text: Most new businesses fail within a few years, but the founders often go on to succeed with later projects. What they learn from failure appears to be as valuable as any early funding.

title: The inner lives of animals
text: Scientists were once reluctant to say that animals had emotions. Today, studies of elephants, dogs and even fish suggest that the inner lives of animals are richer than we assumed.

title: A city's soundtrack
text: Every city has its own soundtrack: the calls of street vendors, the rhythm of motorbikes, the bells of a distant temple. Visitors often remember these sounds long after they have forgotten the sights.
cues: Keep the rhythm of the list steady.

title: What separates champions
text: Top athletes are often admired for their talent, but what separates them is usually less visible: years of repetition, careful recovery and the discipline to rest when they would rather train.

title: Renting into our thirties
text: In many countries, owning a home was once seen as a natural step into adulthood. Rising prices have made that step much harder, and many young people now rent well into their thirties.

title: Winter light
text: Shorter days in winter can affect people's energy and mood more than they expect. Spending time outdoors in daylight, even briefly, is one of the simplest ways to counter the effect.

title: Pause before you share
text: False stories often spread faster than corrections because they are designed to provoke strong emotions. Pausing before sharing something shocking is a small habit with surprisingly large effects.

title: What a mentor does
text: A good mentor does not provide all the answers. Instead, they ask the kind of questions that help you discover what you already know and notice what you have been avoiding.

title: Patterns in history
text: History does not repeat itself exactly, but patterns do recur. Studying them will not predict the future; it can, however, make us more alert to familiar warning signs.

title: Technology in the classroom
text: Evaluate the role technology should play in education.
cues: Where does it genuinely help learning?
Where can it distract or replace thinking?
How should teachers decide when to use it?

title: Global and local cultures
text: Discuss whether globalisation threatens local cultures.

title: Who protects the environment?
text: Who should take the greatest responsibility for protecting the environment: governments, businesses or individuals?

text: Discuss the relationship between success and happiness.

text: Discuss whether privacy is still possible in the digital age.

text: Discuss the gap in opportunities between cities and rural areas.

title: Sport and national identity
text: Discuss why sport matters so much to national identity.

text: Discuss how communities can adapt to a changing climate.

title: Public money for the arts
text: Discuss whether public money should be spent on the arts.

title: The internet in remote places
text: Discuss how internet access changes life in remote communities.

title: A careful "it depends"
text: Experts are often most persuasive when they sound certain, yet the most honest answer to a complex question is frequently a qualified one. Learning to trust a careful "it depends" may be one of the subtler skills of adult life.

title: The translator's balance
text: A translator is forever negotiating between faithfulness and readability. Render a sentence too literally and it sounds foreign; adapt it too freely and the author's voice disappears beneath the translator's own.

title: When attention is the product
text: When a service is free, our attention is usually the product being sold. Every notification competes for a resource that is finite, and the companies that capture it most effectively are rewarded handsomely.

title: The selective past
text: Nostalgia is curiously selective. It edits out the inconvenience and anxiety of the past, leaving a softened version that can make the present seem poorer than it really is.

title: Layers of a city
text: Old cities resemble manuscripts that have been written over many times. Beneath a modern shopping street you may find the outline of a medieval market, and beneath that, traces of a settlement no one remembers.
cues: Keep a steady rhythm through the long sentence.

title: The hidden cost of flexibility
text: Flexibility at work is generally welcomed, but it carries a hidden cost: when every hour could be working time, it becomes harder to justify any hour that is not.

title: Speaking about uncertainty
text: Patients often want a definite diagnosis, while doctors must weigh probabilities. Communicating that uncertainty honestly, without causing unnecessary alarm, is one of the most demanding parts of medical practice.

title: Stepping back from nature
text: Rewilding asks a provocative question: what if, instead of managing nature so tightly, we stepped back and allowed natural processes to reshape the land? The answer, in several projects, has been a surprising return of wildlife.

title: Stage sets for tourists
text: Travel broadens the mind, we are told, but mass tourism can also flatten the places it celebrates. Neighbourhoods become stage sets, and the residents who gave them character are gradually priced out.

title: Private fortunes, public problems
text: Generous donations by the very rich are rightly welcomed, yet they raise an uncomfortable question about accountability: should private fortunes decide which public problems receive attention first?

title: Persuasion that does not feel like it
text: The most effective persuasion rarely feels like persuasion at all. It works by framing a choice so that one option seems natural and the other faintly unreasonable.

title: The notes left out
text: Musicians often say that the notes they leave out matter as much as those they play. A well-placed silence gives the listener time to anticipate, and anticipation is half the pleasure of music.

title: Recipes and memory
text: What we eat is rarely just a matter of taste. Recipes carry memories of migration, scarcity and celebration, which is why a single dish can provoke surprisingly fierce arguments about authenticity.

title: The promise of merit
text: A meritocracy promises that talent and effort will be rewarded. Its critics point out, however, that those who succeed often credit their own merit while overlooking the advantages that smoothed their path.

title: What data cannot explain
text: Data can describe what people do with remarkable precision, but it struggles to explain why they do it. Without that understanding, decisions based purely on numbers risk being efficient and wrong at the same time.

title: Learning to judge danger
text: Children today are supervised more closely than any previous generation. The intention is protective, but some researchers argue that free play, with its small risks, is precisely how children learn to judge danger.

title: Monuments and memory
text: Monuments tell us less about the past than about the people who chose to build them. Each statue reflects a decision about who deserved to be remembered and, by implication, who did not.

title: Judging a fish by climbing
text: Measuring animal intelligence by human standards is a little like judging a fish by its ability to climb a tree. Each species has developed the abilities its environment demanded.

title: The winters we remember
text: Oddly, we remember the weather of our childhood as more extreme than the records suggest: summers longer, snow deeper. Memory, it seems, prefers a good story to an accurate one.
cues: Contrast a good story and an accurate one.

title: How a house becomes a home
text: A house becomes a home not through its furniture but through repetition: the same chair by the window, the same creak on the stairs, the familiar sounds of other people moving through the rooms.

title: The hours lost travelling
text: Long commutes are one of the few costs people consistently underestimate when choosing where to live. A larger house rarely makes up for the hours lost every week travelling to and from it.

title: The engine of science
text: Doubt is often treated as a weakness, but in science it is the engine of progress. A theory earns our confidence only after surviving determined attempts to prove it wrong.

title: Experts and beginners
text: The more people learn about a field, the more aware they become of what they do not know. Genuine experts are therefore often more cautious in their claims than confident beginners.

title: Suggestion, not statement
text: Advertising rarely lies outright; it prefers suggestion. A product is placed beside happiness, freedom or success, and the viewer is left to draw the connection that the advertiser cannot legally state.

title: A few kilometres apart
text: Life expectancy can differ by years between neighbourhoods only a few kilometres apart. Such gaps reflect not personal choices alone but housing, income, education and access to care.

title: Can anyone be objective?
text: Discuss whether journalists, historians or scientists can ever be fully objective.
cues: Is objectivity still a useful goal?

title: How much do we control?
text: Discuss how much control people really have over the course of their lives.
